prize_parts.citation: For a compressed, intensely worked French prose that, across a deliberately concentrated body of work, turns obscure lives and the making of art into narrative inquiry into vocation, power and anonymity.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Michon first, with Cărtărescu and Wright as alternatives. The exchange did not weaken the case, but it did make me state its basis more precisely. The case is voice, meaning a sentence whose syntax and diction are worked so closely that it is hard to attribute to anyone else, joined to a recurring subject. As publicly known, that subject is what vocation costs, how the minor and forgotten are given form, and how art and power relate. Small Lives and The Eleven are the representative works. The shorter books on Rimbaud and on a painter's or a king's life, as I understand them from public knowledge, return to the same questions with a different matter each time. That is a reason to think the method renews itself within a narrow field rather than repeating one success. Sem-Sandberg's distinction is useful. A compact oeuvre can show sustained quality through consistency, but significance across the whole body of work is the harder criterion, and the committee must argue it from the sentences and the structure, not from corpus size or from how many colleagues rank him. I hold that significance rests on the unity of formal compression and subject, which I find unusually complete. I would keep the citation to that unity and make no claim that Michon represents French prose generally. I have not independently verified any text, and my judgment rests on public knowledge and on translation.
statement.case_against: The breadth objection is real and I have not answered it conclusively. A small corpus built on one method asks the whole-oeuvre criterion to carry a lot, and Sward and Palm are right that it is a harder test than a longer record. A second reservation is that much of the effect lies in the French sentence, so the committee may admire what it can only partly judge. A third is that I know the later and shorter books less well than the two best-known titles, and if they only restate the early manner, the objection gets stronger. Cărtărescu offers a longer record from which to judge a sustained project, and if the committee could show that Blinding and Solenoid differ in structure and sentence, I would have to weigh that seriously against my own preference. I have not seen that shown, only asserted on public knowledge.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first and Michon fifth. She accepts Michon's formal concentration but finds the whole-oeuvre criterion harder to meet with a deliberately small corpus, and says Cărtărescu gives more work across more years from which to judge sustained quality.
responses.response: I accept that a longer record makes it easier to show a project sustained over time, and I do not think the size objection can be waved away. But more years and more pages are not the same as demonstrated renewal, and you yourself say you cannot settle that without closer comparison of the volumes. My answer is that Michon's returns to vocation, anonymity and the afterlife of lives look to me like deepening, not repetition, although I hold that from public knowledge and translation. We also agree that the translation caveat applies to both of us. I would ask that it not lower the writer whose effect lies in syntax more than the one whose architecture might survive translation better. I cannot judge that second claim, and I would want it tested on passages and not assumed.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and Michon second. She grants Michon's exceptional concentration but says a small corpus makes it harder to show more than a few perfect books. She proposes that the committee name what changes between Blinding and Solenoid, and she keeps thematic affinity out of the argument.
responses.response: I agree that thematic affinity with art and vocation is not a literary criterion, and I have tried to rest the case on the prose. The challenge about a few perfect books is fair, and I turn it back with respect. The test of what changes between volumes should apply to Michon too: what do the books after Small Lives and The Eleven add in range, and what is the sentence doing differently? I cannot fully answer that and say so. Your reading that the large Cărtărescu books enlarge the world rather than restate it is the strongest answer to my own repetition worry, and I count it. It still rests on public knowledge. If the committee can name the structural difference between Blinding and Solenoid, I will treat Cărtărescu as the closer rival.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Michon first. He frames a four-decade method held without visible dilution as sustained quality, but says this does not settle significance, and he wants that argued in committee on the sentences and structure of both writers, not on their size.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and take it as the standard for round 2. Consistency answers sustained quality. Significance is a separate claim, and the committee must earn it by looking at the sentences. I would offer the same test to Cărtărescu and Wright. Your question about whether the later and shorter books add anything is also mine, and I do not want to hide behind the two famous titles. If the later books only repeat the early manner, the citation should be narrowed or the preference reconsidered. For now I read them as the same inquiry applied to new matter, not as thinning, but I cannot call that verified.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first and Michon third. He asks whether the committee can find evidence of what Adonis's poems do at the level of the line, kept separate from reception and from the essays, and he says neither of us can judge Michon's prose or Adonis's verse directly.
responses.response: I agree that neither of us can judge the French sentence or the Arabic line directly, and I think the honest consequence is that translation risk should be a common discount, not a reason to favor one language. Where we differ is in how far a committee can compensate. For Michon the committee has several translations and a body of critical commentary to compare against the French. For Adonis you rightly ask for specialist reading of the originals. I would support obtaining that for any poet who reaches the final vote. Your point that the claim concerns the sustained shaping of a poetic language across decades, not each late collection matching the early landmarks, is fair and I would apply the same logic to Michon. I remain unable to put Adonis above Michon because I can test the prose case more directly, but that is a judgment about my access and not a verdict on Adonis, whom I ranked low for that reason.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text. My view of Michon rests on public knowledge of Small Lives, The Eleven and the shorter books, and on translation.
It is unresolved whether a deliberately compact oeuvre carries enough breadth and significance for a whole-oeuvre citation.
How much of the effect of Michon's French sentence survives translation, and how far the committee can compensate with the original, is uncertain.
I know Michon's later and shorter books less well than the two best-known titles, and I cannot say whether they add range or restate the early manner.
I cannot judge whether Cărtărescu's very long forms extend or restate the earlier cycle, nor whether his dense Romanian survives translation better or worse than Michon's French.
Wright's Indigenous idiom and oral rhythm and her later work are hard for me to assess, and Adonis's Arabic prosody cannot be judged without specialist reading of the originals.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no connection to any shortlisted writer. My own work as a novelist of historical fiction with real people, and as a critic, is context only and is not evidence of a preference for Michon or anyone else. No round-1 exchange changed this disclosure.
